verses.text: When it was decided that we would sail for Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, who belonged to the Imperial Regiment.
We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was about to sail for ports along the coast of Asia. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, came with us.
The next day we stopped at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and let him visit his friends so they could provide for him.
From there we put out to sea and sailed under the sheltered side of Cyprus because the winds were against us.
After sailing across the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we reached Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put us aboard it.
We sailed slowly for many days and had difficulty reaching a point across from Cnidus. Since the wind wouldn’t let us continue that way, we sailed under the sheltered side of Crete, opposite Salmone.
We struggled along the coast and reached a place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.
A lot of time had passed, and sailing had become dangerous because the Fast had already passed. So Paul warned them,
saying, “Men, I can see this voyage is going to bring injury and heavy loss—not only to the cargo and ship, but to our lives too.”
But the centurion trusted the ship’s captain and owner more than Paul’s warning.

Since the harbor wasn’t suitable for wintering, most people advised sailing on, hoping they could reach Phoenix and spend the winter there. Phoenix was a harbor in Crete, facing southwest and northwest.
When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had what they wanted. They pulled up anchor and sailed close along the shore of Crete.
But before long, a violent wind called the Northeaster swept down from the island.
The ship was caught in the storm and couldn’t face the wind, so we gave in and were driven along.
We sailed under the shelter of a small island called Clauda and managed, with difficulty, to secure the ship’s lifeboat.
After hauling it aboard, they used ropes to reinforce the ship. Afraid they’d run aground on the sandbars of Syrtis, they lowered the sea anchor and let the wind drive us along.
The storm battered us so badly that the next day they began throwing cargo overboard.
On the third day, they threw the ship’s equipment overboard with their own hands.
For many days we saw neither sun nor stars, and the storm kept raging. At last, all hope that we’d be saved was gone.
After they’d gone a long time without food, Paul stood among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not sailed from Crete. Then we wouldn’t have suffered this damage and loss.
But now I urge you: Take heart! None of you will lose your life. Only the ship will be lost.
Last night an angel from the God I belong to and serve stood beside me
and said, ‘Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. And God has graciously given you everyone sailing with you.’
“So take heart, men! I trust God that it will happen just as he told me.
But we must run aground on an island.”
On the fourteenth night, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, the sailors sensed around midnight that land was near.
They took soundings and found twenty fathoms. A little later they took soundings again and found fifteen fathoms.
Afraid we’d hit rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daylight.
The sailors tried to escape from the ship. They lowered the lifeboat into the sea, pretending they were going to put out anchors from the bow.
Paul told the centurion and soldiers, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you can’t be saved.”
So the soldiers cut the lifeboat’s ropes and let it drift away.
Just before dawn, Paul urged everyone to eat. He said, “For fourteen days you’ve been waiting anxiously and going without food—you haven’t eaten anything.
So I urge you to eat something. You need it to survive. Not one of you will lose even a hair from your head.”
After saying this, he took bread, thanked God in front of everyone, broke it, and began to eat.
Then everyone was encouraged and ate some food too.
There were 276 of us on the ship in all.
After they’d eaten enough, they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea.
When daylight came, they didn’t recognize the land, but they saw a bay with a beach and decided to try to run the ship aground there.
They cut loose the anchors and left them in the sea. At the same time, they untied the rudder ropes, hoisted the foresail to the wind, and headed for the beach.
But they hit a sandbar where two currents met and ran the ship aground. The bow stuck fast and wouldn’t move, while the stern began breaking apart under the force of the waves.
The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so none could swim away and escape.
But the centurion wanted to save Paul, so he stopped them. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for land,
and the rest to follow on planks or pieces of the ship. In this way, everyone reached land safely.
